title: Manuel Gustavo Pinedo-Cuba
text: I am a physicist working on the experimental study of transition-metal oxides, currently based in the Oxide Nanophysics group at the Catalan Institute of Nanoscience and Nanotechnology (ICN2) in Barcelona. My work sits at the interface between materials growth, low-temperature electrical transport, and the instrumentation that makes those measurements possible.

title: Manuel Gustavo Pinedo-Cuba
text:
What I work on
Much of my day-to-day revolves around cryogenic transport measurements of oxide thin films and heterostructures — resistance-versus-temperature curves, Hall effect, and field-dependent transport down to low temperatures and under applied magnetic field. I am particularly interested in metal–insulator transitions and how they are shaped by strain, dimensionality, and interface effects in systems such as nickelates and doped titanates.
Alongside the physics, I build a good deal of the measurement infrastructure I rely on: instrument drivers for lock-in amplifiers, temperature controllers and magnet power supplies, a multi-threaded control application for coordinating an experiment end to end, and Python tooling for extracting physical quantities from the raw data. I find that caring about the measurement chain — not just the final plot — tends to pay off in the quality of the science.

title: Manuel Gustavo Pinedo-Cuba
text:
Background
I completed my undergraduate and master’s studies in physics at the Universidad Nacional Mayor de San Marcos in Lima, with a focus on condensed matter and materials science, working on thin-film growth by sputtering and pulsed laser deposition. That experimental grounding — sample preparation, X-ray diffraction, magnetometry — is what I now bring to the study of oxide nanostructures.

title: Manuel Gustavo Pinedo-Cuba
text:
Get in touch
I am always glad to talk with people working on oxide electronics, metal–insulator transitions, cryogenic instrumentation, or the messy-but-rewarding business of making reliable transport measurements. You will find my publications and full background on the CV page, and shorter technical write-ups in Notes.

title: The Fourier transform as a change of basis in L^2
text:
We usually meet the Fourier transform as a formula,

\hat{f}(\xi) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\, e^{-2\pi i x \xi}\, \mathrm{d}x ,

but this hides the structural idea. The transform is better understood as a change of orthonormal basis in the Hilbert space L^2(\mathbb{R}).

title: The Fourier transform as a change of basis in L^2
text:
We usually meet the Fourier transform as a formula,

\hat{f}(\xi) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\, e^{-2\pi i x \xi}\, \mathrm{d}x ,

but this hides the structural idea. The transform is better understood as a change of orthonormal basis in the Hilbert space L^2(\mathbb{R}).

title: The Fourier transform as a change of basis in L^2
text:
Vectors and functions
In \mathbb{R}^n a vector \mathbf{v} is expanded in an orthonormal basis \{\mathbf{e}_k\} as

\mathbf{v} = \sum_k \langle \mathbf{e}_k, \mathbf{v}\rangle\, \mathbf{e}_k .

A function f \in L^2 behaves the same way, with the inner product

\langle g, f\rangle = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \overline{g(x)}\, f(x)\, \mathrm{d}x .

The complex exponentials e_\xi(x) = e^{2\pi i x \xi} play the role of the basis vectors \mathbf{e}_k. The Fourier coefficient \hat{f}(\xi) is nothing but the projection \langle e_\xi, f\rangle.

title: The Fourier transform as a change of basis in L^2
text:
Why this matters
Because the transform is a unitary map, it preserves inner products — this is Parseval’s theorem,

\int |f(x)|^2\, \mathrm{d}x = \int |\hat{f}(\xi)|^2\, \mathrm{d}\xi ,

which is simply the statement that a rotation of the basis does not change the length of a vector.
